Permeable Pavement: Letting Rain Through Instead of Off

Conventional pavement is designed to shed water quickly, directing rain
into gutters and storm drains. Permeable pavement takes the opposite
approach: it is built to let water pass through the surface itself and
soak into a layered base beneath, reducing the volume of runoff that
reaches storm sewers during a storm.

Common Forms

Three general types are in wide use. Porous asphalt and pervious concrete
look similar to their conventional counterparts but contain interconnected
voids that let water drain through the material itself. Permeable
interlocking pavers are individual units, often concrete or stone, laid
with small gaps between them that are filled with gravel or coarse sand
rather than mortar, allowing water to flow between the units into the base
below.

The Base Layer Does the Real Work

Underneath any permeable surface sits a bed of graded stone, typically
ranging from fine gravel near the surface to larger stone deeper down.
This layer serves two purposes: it provides structural support so the
pavement can carry traffic, and it acts as a temporary reservoir, holding
water so it can infiltrate into the native soil gradually rather than all
at once. In some designs, an underdrain pipe near the bottom of the base
carries any excess water to a conventional storm system once the reservoir
is full, acting as an overflow rather than the primary drainage path.

Maintenance Considerations

The voids and gaps that let water through are also the pavement's main
vulnerability: fine sediment, leaves, and dirt can clog them over time,
gradually reducing how much water infiltrates. Regular vacuum sweeping —
rather than the pressure washing used on conventional pavement, which can
force debris deeper into the material — is the typical upkeep routine,
along with keeping adjacent landscaping from washing loose soil onto the
surface.

Where It Fits

Permeable pavement is most often used in parking lots, low-traffic
residential streets, plazas, and walkways, where structural demands are
moderate. It is one tool among several — alongside rain gardens, vegetated
swales, and retention ponds — that planners group under the broader label
of green stormwater infrastructure, all aimed at managing rain closer to
where it falls instead of routing it away as fast as possible.
